HStar builds heavy-class, reusable spaceships and develops heavy-capable, global spaceports to sell launch services to customers around the world.

The HStar rocket is capable of unlocking the next phase of industry by deploying the biggest projects that will solve tomorrow’s problems on earth and accelerate many technological transitions.

HStar is a French-US initiative where both countries contribute to finance and build the global solution for worldwide application.

The HStar rocket uses proven technology which fills an undersupplied gap in the global launch market. It is an ITAR-free, non-dependent heavy launch capability using European very high thrust engines. A patent has been registered for France and Europe application.

HStar is a cohesive team with domain expertise building rockets and spacecraft. The company employs an experienced & proven team (eg. Kineis/CNES, SES, Eutelsat, ArianeGroup, SpaceX, NASA, etc). The team has developed a detailed, multi-horizon path to build Europe’s very heavy launcher, and then expand to sell global launch transportation services to the growing demand.

HStar leverages a public-private partnership model with key European partners and champions as well as European Member States to provide European response to US launch dominance. The distinct position among launch providers utilizes a lowest-risk, systems-integration approach. The company will provide global launch with spaceport partnerships, starting in French Guiana, the US, and Australia.

HStar has an accelerated path to first orbital launch in 2032, and launch services capable of one to two launches per week by 2036.

entityDescription:
The Chair of Satellite Geodesy is one of six departments within the Institute of Geomatics at the Faculty of Geodesy. Faculty members of the Chair include: Željko Bačić, PhD (Full Professor), Danijel Šugar, PhD (Associate Professor), Zvonimir Nevistić, PhD (Post.Doc researcher), Petar Jelić, MSc. (Assistant). 
The core areas of the Chair's activities cover all aspects of satellite positioning, space geodesy and geodetic astronomy, as well as the integration of space technologies with other sensors, and systems. The Chair’s educational activities are organized through seven compulsory and elective courses. At the undergraduate level: "Satellite Positioning", "Geodetic Astronomy" and “Engineering Informatics” and at the graduate level of Geodesy and Geoinformatics: "Navigation", "Integrated Systems in Geomatics", "Space Geodesy," "Satellite Geodesy - Project" and "Geodetic Astronomy - Project". 
The Chair's scientific and professional work focuses on the disciplines and courses it covers. In addition to these areas, Chair staff are actively involved in research on the application of GNSS for geodetic and non-geodetic purposes, investigating the effects of GNSS interference, monitoring the influence of the ionosphere on GNSS measurements, spatial data infrastructure, disaster risk reduction, drone applications, indoor navigation, application of spatial data in new concepts such as smart cities and digital twins and remote sensing.
The results of the Chair's work are reflected in a large number and wide range of published papers and participation in international and domestic conferences as well as leadership and participation in numerous scientific, professional, and educational projects (Erasmus+ CHBE and Strategic partnership). Chair staff lead and actively participate in the Copernicus Academy and Relay Croatia organizations and promoting space technologies in the Republic of Croatia through various channels.

entityDescription: Human in Motion Robotics (HMR) is a Canadian pioneer in developing next-generation exoskeleton technology rooted in advanced humanoid robotics and AI. Supported by a world-class team of engineers, scientists, and clinicians, HMR has created XoMotion™, an innovative lower-limb robotic exoskeleton designed to deliver superior rehabilitation outcomes that surpass the capabilities of existing technologies in the current rehabilitation model. XoMotion is the world’s most advanced wearable robotic exoskeleton, designed to assist individuals with mobility impairments due to spinal cord injuries, stroke, and other neurological conditions in standing up and walking. This humanoid robotics-based medical device offers unparalleled multi-directional locomotion support through self-balancing and hands-free functionality, enabling customizable and task-oriented robotic rehabilitation treatments across various stages of recovery. entityDescription: The Seatizens for Plankton Planet (S4P2) Association is a non-profit non-governmental organization governed by French law, specifically the 1901 law on associations. Founded in 2016 during the pilot phase of the Plankton Planet project (Vargas et al., 2022, Frontiers in Marine Science), S4P2 brings together “seatizens”— i.e. all sorts of seafarers and sea users - who are eager to discover, measure, and understand the invisible living majority in the oceans: plankton or the ocean microbiome. The Association has two primary missions: (i) ocean microbiome literacy to raise awareness about planktonic ecosystems, and (ii) the recruitment, training, and coordination of seatizens to build up a cooperative, cost-effective, and sustainable global measurement of aquatic microscopic life. Overall, the goal of the Plankton Planet initiative (in which S4P2 is one of the running entity) is to establish, by 2030, the first seatizen-based standard measure of the surface ocean microbiome across planetary scales, allowing to monitor and understand the evolution and health of the ocean.

The Professorship for Space Technology focuses its research on three main areas: Nanosatellites for Extraterrestrial Missions, Space Systems & Higher Autonomy, and UAP & SETI Research.

Key achievements include the fully in-house developed, built, and operated nanosatellite missions SONATE and SONATE-2. SONATE-2, a 6U+ satellite launched in 2024, integrates AI technologies for in-orbit training and features an electric propulsion system and a novell star tracker, building on the experiences and components of its predecessor. The earlier SONATE mission pioneered autonomy in nanosatellites with systems like ASAP-Light for automated event detection and ADIA-Light for onboard diagnostics.

The professorship also operates a remote-controlled telescope in Spain for the detection of lunar transient phenomena, a telescope in Würzburg for SSA research, and a SkyCam-System for UAP detection. Additional expertise includes the design, construction, and operation of star trackers and subsystems for small satellites, as well as research into autorotative landing systems for interplanetary missions.

entityDescription:
The Baltic Marine Environment Protection Commission – also known as the “Helsinki Commission” or “HELCOM” – was established in 1974 pursuant to and at the same time as theConvention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Baltic Sea Area(the “Helsinki Convention”).
The Helsinki Commission meets annually, with allContracting Partiesparticipating: Denmark, Estonia, the European Union, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia and Sweden. In addition, meetings at the Ministerial level are held every few years (usually every three years). The Contracting Parties are represented by Heads of Delegation (HOD).
The Commission adoptsRecommendationsrelated to the protection of the marine environment and sustainable maritime activities, decides on the budget and makes other key decisions. Decisions are made by consensus.
Thechairmanshipof the Commission rotates between the Contracting Parties every two years, according to their alphabetical order in English, the working language of the Commission.
The working structure of HELCOM consists of the meetings of the Helsinki Commission, the Heads of Delegation, and the eight mainHELCOM Working Groups. The HELCOM work and meetings are coordinated by the HELCOM Secretariat.

The HELCOM Secretariat coordinates the work and meetings of the Helsinki Commission, and ensures that theContracting Partiesmeet their obligations under theHelsinki Convention. The headquarters of HELCOM, the Secretariat, is located in Helsinki, Finland.

entityDescription: Herobots is an innovative startup focused on developing soft robotics solutions for extreme applications. Soft robotics represents a new frontier in robotics, enabling the execution of remote operations in confined and inaccessible environments where conventional robots cannot operate, with significant applications in the nuclear and space sectors. In these fields, there is a pressing need for solutions aimed at decommissioning, such as dismantling old nuclear facilities or decommissioning obsolete satellites, to support the green transition. To address this, Herobots proposes the use of long-reach soft robots capable of accessing confined spaces and performing operations with precision. However, the flexibility of these robots can pose challenges, such as positioning errors and unwanted vibrations if not properly controlled. To overcome this issue, Herobots has developed a series of software tools for predicting their mechanical behavior and for active control, helping remote operators safely teleoperate the robots.
